rv.q: Then grab your coat, get out of the house and lose your cares at this totally enchanting show.
As Harold Hill in a glorious and exuberant new revival of 'The Music Man,' Jackman is like a coiled spring, effortlessly leaping onto desks.
In its determined effort to evoke the musical comedy Broadway of yore and make us feel happy simply to be in a theater again, the show ironically feels urgently timely.
As cheeseball and predictable as The Music Man might be, it will still surprise you.
Hugh Jackman and Sutton Foster bring their considerable star power and musical-theater chops to this handsome, old-fashioned revival
Hugh Jackman and Sutton Foster are so winning in the leads that they manage to paper over some of the production's shortcomings
It was what Broadway was meant to be – an evening to escape to a time that never was and always will be.
The Music Man lives up to every expectation except the most crucial one: Surprise.
Instead we get an extremely neat, generally perky, overly cautious take on a musical that, being about the con game of love and music, needs more danger in the telling.
That just can’t fully drive a show far more complex than the usual romantic musical.
Yet while this Music Man is a solid and professional piece of work, and includes many incidental pleasures, the hoped-for enchantment never arrives.
“The Music Man,” I’m sorry to say, does not live up to our oversize expectations.

More’s the pity, then, that this undeniably polished production, with its ticket-sales-galvanizing star, Hugh Jackman, proves to be a sadly mechanical, overproduced and overdesigned revival of a musical that needs tender care to allow its undeniable charms to bloom.
This revival has been in the works seemingly forever.

So, scrubbed clean of anything that might offend the supersensitive, costing as much as a cross-country flight, and, in some views, lacking the chiaroscuro of darkness mingled with light, The Music Man still comes out a winner.
On the other hand, it doesn’t quite rise to blue-ribbon garden-show winner.

"4/5 stars...The production is dazzling and enjoyable and does what it’s supposed to do: keeps the audience enraptured and brings them to their feet in response to a heart-tugging curtain call featuring a bubbly cast...And yet (yes, there is an 'and yet'), this is not a perfect 'Music Man.' The problem is with the two leads...
This slightly zany production sells the show's intelligent warmth with a persuasiveness to rival Harold Hill himself.
A good time is all but guaranteed -- if you don't mind a pair of questionably cast stars and some unwanted textual tampering.
Are there soothing and satisfying pleasures in familiarity, high voltage, and expert execution?
Jackman and Foster are magnetic together, their chemistry undeniable as they dance and sing their way through Meredith Willson's beloved musical.
Sutton and Jackman are having such a good time bringing their characters to each other that the rest of the choppy story doesn’t matter.
Yes, she loves him, even if your final thought may be not happiness they are together but that she is worthy of so much better.
Director Jerry Zaks’ production is a throwback in just about every sense, for good and for bad.
Even so, The Music Man is only held together by a string of memorable and beloved songs for which we patiently wait.

It's a perfectly enjoyable, not life-changing staging of a classic musical, and if you're looking for a night out that takes you away from the February doldrums, however briefly, this Music Man is a sight for sore eyes.
Everything onstage is pure Broadway gold, fine-tuned to the gods and played to the back of the house.
The result, for all the production’s star quality, eye-catching choreography, and professional gloss, is at best a missed opportunity.
The result is a weirdly flat production that rarely transcends its base g
But as the consummate con artist and showman Harold Hill, Jackman, Jackman displays little more than peppy cheer and easy charm.
As such, the show remains a big disappointment considering the amount of talent that has gone into the new production.
So, it’s OK fantasy, if you still believe in stories of the fifties.
Everything about this revival of The Music Man felt generic, it never justified its existence.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this star-powered revival: some praise Jackman and Foster's charisma and the show's exuberant spectacle, while others find it a bloated, uninspired letdown that doesn't live up to massive expectations.

sg.ra: With a 44'10" proscenium and a stage wider than most Broadway houses, Orchestra Center C-G is the only zone where you get the full picture head-on without sacrificing actor-face detail. Spectacle-heavy productions here (BTTF's DeLorean, Mamma Mia! dance numbers) are blocked edge-to-edge, so off-center seats lose pieces even a few rows in.

This is the house's quiet value zone: full center alignment matters more here than proximity does because the auditorium is wider than deep, so row V center still reads front-on. Last orchestra row is short (~6 seats) with unusual legroom per multiple patrons. Tradeoff specific to Winter Garden: the mezzanine overhang starts around row O per published guides, clipping the top of the stage — fine for naturalistic plays, worse for musicals with fly-in sets.

Wide-house penalty hits hardest here: because the auditorium is broader than deep, side-orchestra angles into the stage are sharper than in a typical Broadway house — the further out you sit, the more the upstage far corner disappears. Multiple patrons specifically call out stage-right pillars clipping their view on Salesman; works better for plays where action holds center than for musicals with full-stage choreography.

In a wider-than-deep house the front center mezzanine rescues the seat selection by giving you the one thing center orchestra can't: altitude to take in the full 44'10" proscenium at once. Multiple patrons specifically cite this row range for Mamma Mia! and BTTF over the rear orchestra, and it avoids both the pillar risk on the sides and the mezz overhang clipping rear stalls.

Wide-house geometry pushes the far-left and far-right mezz off at a sharp angle — the stage-opposite corner is the consistent casualty. Reviewers note the speaker stacks on the edge as a recurring blocker, and because the mezz is only ~9 rows deep, distance isn't the killer — angle is. Good option if you're watching a show where the action centers; poor for full-stage choreography.

sg.n: Box Seats (Box B, C, F, G)
sg.ra: The Winter Garden boxes are widely flagged as among the most obstructed in Broadway — the box structure itself blocks significant stage area and the side angle compounds it. Skip at any price.
